title: Giant isolated splenic hydatidosis
case_text:
A 30-year-old female patient presented with complaints of fever, breathlessness, dull-aching, continuous pain, and dragging sensation on the left side of the abdomen since 3 months. Also, there was history of loss of weight and appetite. Past history was insignificant. On examination, abdomen was slightly distended with a palpable mass reaching up to the umbilicus, 6-7 cm from the left costal margin. The mass was tender, firm, irregular and fingers could not be insinuated below the ribs. A systemic examination was normal. Routine investigations revealed leucocytosis (Total leukocyte count=12,000/mm3) with eosinophilia (7%, absolute eosinophil count=840/mm3) and raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (35 mm in first hour). An X-ray study of both abdomen and chest was found to be normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen showed enlarged spleen with multiple cystic areas, together measuring 18x15x11 cm. [Figure 1]. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed a large mass measuring 17.5x15x10 cm, containing air fluid levels and heterogeneous contents with predominant low-density areas, elevating left dome of the diaphragm [Figure 2]. Other abdominal organs were found to be normal. Therefore, the clinical diagnosis of the cystic lesion of spleen was made.
Left subcostal exploratory laparotomy was performed revealing huge cystic mass occupying lower pole of spleen. Splenectomy was performed and sent for HPE. Tab. Mebendazole 200 mg/kg/day was started on fifth post operative day and continued after surgery for three months.
Grossly, the splenectomy specimen measured 17x14x10 cm. The posterior aspect showed a cystic cavity having a white and smooth cyst wall, filled with multiple, variable-sized daughter cysts in a flower-shaped arrangement [Figure 3]. The hematoxylin and eosin (H and E)-stained slides showed a cyst wall comprising of three layers [Figure 4]. The cystic contents consisted of mixture of multiple infolded membranes, fragmented hooklets, and debris which were part of hydatid sand. Multiple scolices of Echinococcus granulosus were also seen [Figure 5]. Definitive diagnosis of a hydatid cyst was, hence, made.

   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: giant isolated splenic hydatid cyst
